claim: A pending CRASH note is lost when a call is cancelled after it reached the toolset. `#forward` empties `#notice` into the answer of a cancelled request, and the stdio binder never writes that answer. This breaks A3 (every pending loss is carried), the guide sentence "Every pending loss is reported" (guides/browser.md:2333), and the U7 report's claim that the server "retains every pending loss note".
evidence: After execute, three paths call `#annotate` without checking `context.signal`: line 319 (UNRESOLVED), line 327 (`throw new BrowserError(this.#annotate(result.error, slot))`), and line 329 (string success). Line 310 checks the abort only to decide whether to ping. `#annotate` (lines 332-341) runs `this.#notice.delete(lost)` for every note it renders. The refusal path guards this case at line 293 (`context.signal.throwIfAborted()` before `#annotate`), so the post-execute paths are inconsistent with it. mcp src/core/helpers.ts:1887-1889: `if (!request.signal.aborted) await transport.send(answer)`, so a cancelled request writes nothing.
failure_scenario: Size 2. The lease S is killed between calls, and the watch reports it, so `#notice` = {S}. The client sends tools/call `wait` (id 5). `#serve` grants the spare T and the wait runs on T. The client sends notifications/cancelled for id 5. The wait fails with the abort. Line 310 skips the ping, and `#lease.value === T`, so line 327 calls `#annotate(result.error, T)`, which deletes S from `#notice`. The binder discards the answer. Call 6 `look` answers with no `BROWSER_SERVER_CRASH` line, so the agent keeps the old URL and the stale eN references from S in its model. The same loss happens when a string-valued tool finishes after the cancel (line 329). Fix: right after execute, and before any `#annotate`, run `context.signal.throwIfAborted()` (or skip annotating when the signal has aborted) so that the notes stay pending. Add a src:server case: a pending note, then a cancelled call on the successor, then assert that the next call opens with `BROWSER_SERVER_CRASH:`.

verdict.reason: Lane: objective. I traced the failure myself. A tool call cancelled after `#serve` returns still runs `#annotate` on its result, and `#annotate` deletes every note it renders. The mcp binder then drops the answer of an aborted request, so the CRASH note is never delivered. The design says a pending note is cleared only by an outcome or a refusal that carries it (pool-design-3.md:215), and A3 says the note carries every pending loss. No accepted tension (T2-T20) covers a cancelled call. Fix at C:\Users\mikes\WebstormProjects\browser\src\server\BrowserMCPServer.ts:309. Right after execute, and before any `#annotate` call, add `context.signal.throwIfAborted()`, which mirrors the refusal guard at :293. Add a src:server case: a note is pending, a call on the successor is cancelled, and the next call opens with `BROWSER_SERVER_CRASH:`.
verdict.evidence: BrowserMCPServer.ts:291: `#serve` grants the successor T, and nothing consumes `#notice` there. :300: execute runs with `context`, whose signal comes from the request's signal (mcp helpers.ts:745: `AbortSignal.any([options.signal, lifetime])`; binder helpers.ts:1880-1883 passes `request.signal`). :310: the abort is checked only to skip the ping. :317: `#lease?.value === T`, so the throw at :327 is reached. :327 `throw new BrowserError(this.#annotate(result.error, slot))` and :329 `this.#annotate(result.value, slot)` have no abort check. :334-338: `#annotate` iterates `#notice` and calls `this.#notice.delete(lost)` for every slot other than T. mcp helpers.ts:1876: `notifications/cancelled` aborts `request`. :1887-1888: `if (!request.signal.aborted) await transport.send(answer)`, so the answer that carried the note is never written. Trace: S dies between calls, so `#notice`={S}. Call 5 `wait` runs on T, and the client cancels it. The wait fails, :327 deletes S, and the binder discards the answer. Call 6 `look` carries no `BROWSER_SERVER_CRASH`. The same holds when a string-valued tool finishes after the cancel (:329). guides/browser.md:2333 says "Every pending loss is reported", which this path breaks.

evidence: In the `#warm` catch, `this.#write(`browse: ${describeBrowserServerLoss(BROWSER_SERVER_LAUNCH, error)}`)` runs with no `#closing` check. `#destroySlot` guards its own line with `if (this.#closing === undefined) this.#write(...TEARDOWN...)` at :595, and pool-design-3 § Teardown step 3 gives that rule. `#destroy` aborts `#abort` (:233), and the launch receives that signal as `signal: this.#abort.signal` (:541). `Browser.#raceAbort` then rejects with `BrowserConnectionError('Connection aborted')` (Browser.ts:391), and that error reaches this catch. The test 'destroys during a held connect without releasing it or writing afterward' (tests/src/server/BrowserMCPServer.test.ts:675-689) asserts only `fixture.pair.answered` and the profiles directory, never `fixture.log`. The fixture double's held `connect()` rejects with `signal.reason` on abort (tests/setupServer.ts:1664-1676), so the LAUNCH line already reaches the log in that test unobserved.
failure_scenario: An MCP client starts `browse`, then closes stdin while Chromium is still launching, inside the startup window U11 measures. `#end` runs `destroy()`, the abort rejects `connect()`, and stderr receives `browse: BROWSER_SERVER_LAUNCH: Connection aborted.` The process still exits 0. A failed-launch diagnostic appears on a normal shutdown, and no test can see it. The fix is to write the LAUNCH line only when `#closing` is undefined, as :595 does for TEARDOWN, and to assert `fixture.log` is empty in the :675 case.

verdict.reason: I traced it. `destroy()` sets `#closing` in the same turn (BrowserMCPServer.ts:201). `#destroy` then aborts `#abort` (:233). A `#warm` already past its :524 guard has its `connect()` rejected. The real Browser rejects through `#raceAbort` with 'Connection aborted' (Browser.ts:385-392), and the fixture double rejects with `signal.reason` (setupServer.ts:1664-1676). The catch at :568-574 runs `#destroySlot` and then writes the LAUNCH line with no `#closing` check, so a clean shutdown during warming writes `browse: BROWSER_SERVER_LAUNCH: ...`. The closing rule in pool-design-3 § Teardown step 3, which :595 implements, keeps the TEARDOWN line quiet while closing. A10 and A14 cover failed launches, and an abort that shutdown causes is not one of those, so neither ruling covers this line. The test at BrowserMCPServer.test.ts:675-689 asserts only `pair.answered` and the profiles folder, never `fixture.log`, so the line goes unobserved. verdict.evidence: BrowserMCPServer.ts:568-574 calls `this.#write(`browse: ${describeBrowserServerLoss(BROWSER_SERVER_LAUNCH, error)}`)` unconditionally. :595 writes TEARDOWN only `if (this.#closing === undefined)`. :201 sets `#closing` before :233 aborts. setupServer.ts:1670 rejects `connect()` with `signal.reason` on abort. claim: The CRASH note always ends with "The next call acquires a browser that starts at about:blank, or answers BROWSER_SERVER_UNAVAILABLE when none can serve." That sentence is false when the note prefixes an outcome that already ran on the successor. In that case the next call runs on the same successor, in whatever state this call left it. The design gives the F-9 sentence to UNRESOLVED only.
evidence: helpers.ts:94-97 build `next` and return `${message} ${lost} ${next}` for `BROWSER_SERVER_CRASH`. pool-design-3.md:208-213 lists the F-9 "next call acquires…" clause under the interrupted-call text only. Line 721 then asserts `existsSync(folder)` is true, which holds even if the sweep runs.

The loop guard at BrowserMCPServer.ts:611 (`if (this.#closing !== undefined) return`) then returns on the first entry. So the fixed test fails only when both guards are deleted. claim: If the default log `process.stderr` fails with EPIPE during teardown, the process can crash partway through `destroy()`. On POSIX that crash leaves detached browsers running as orphans. The write callback does catch the error, but Node also emits it as an `error` event, and nothing listens for that event. I did not run this; it is traced through Node's stream behavior.
evidence: `#write` passes a callback to `this.#log.write` (lines 655-657) and attaches no `error` listener; ruling A8 forbids one. A socket- or pipe-backed Writable such as `process.stderr` handles a failed write in `onwriteError`, which calls `cb(er)` and then `errorOrDestroy(stream, er)`. With autoDestroy on, that emits `error` on the stream, and an unlistened `error` event throws as an uncaught exception, the familiar `write EPIPE` crash. The U6 log case uses an already destroyed stream (test file lines 1054-1079). Writing to a destroyed stream calls back without emitting `error`, so that case cannot show this path. During teardown a write is reachable through teardown-destructive-2: the aborted warm writes its LAUNCH line before the barrier settles.
failure_scenario: Size 2 on Linux, with the spare still warming. The MCP client is killed, which closes the server's stdin and stderr pipes. stdin `end` triggers `#end`, then `destroy()`, then the abort. The spare's connect rejects, `#warm` writes the LAUNCH line, and the write fails with EPIPE. `process.stderr` emits `error` with no listener, and the process dies before the pool barrier finishes `browser.destroy()` on the lease. The lease's browser was spawned detached (helpers.ts:431), so it survives as an orphan and its `PID-UUID` profile remains until a later start sweeps it. What right looks like: refer to the Orchestrator whether A8 must allow one `error` listener on the log stream, attached for the server's lifetime and routed into `#faults`. Otherwise, the server must write nothing between `#closing` and the end of the barrier (fix teardown-destructive-2). Either way, add a case whose log stream emits `error` on write.

verdict.reason: Most of the trace holds when read. The default log is `process.stderr` (line 147). `#write` adds only a write callback and no `error` listener, as A8 orders ('browse never listens on a stream the host supplies'). Finding 2 confirms that a write is reachable during teardown. The crash itself, though, depends on Node runtime behavior I cannot check by reading. The question is whether a failed write to a pipe-backed `process.stderr` (blocking on POSIX, with `dummyDestroy`) also emits an unhandled `error` event after the callback, and so raises an uncaught exception before the barrier finishes. The orphan claim depends on the same fact, plus the detach off Windows that A13 records. The remedy would breach design ruling A8, which the Orchestrator owns. Refer it to the Orchestrator with a Linux probe: a server whose stderr pipe's reader has closed, then a write.
verdict.evidence: BrowserMCPServer.ts:147 sets `this.#log = options?.log ?? process.stderr`. Lines 653-661: callback only, no listener. design.md:14 (A8) and design.md:19 (A13: detached only off Windows). The U6 case uses a destroyed stream and cannot show the EPIPE emit path.

claim: The U2 cases set a 30 ms deadline on the whole browser instead of on the ping. That deadline also bounds the connect handshake and the target sync. The number is not derived from either case, and it is the timing flake the dispatch reports.
evidence: Both cases build `createBrowser({ cdp: { endpoint: server.endpoint }, timeout: 30 })` (lines 48 and 76). `Browser.#timeout()` (Browser.ts:523-524) feeds that value into several places: `createCDPTransport({ url, timeout })` and `new CDPClient({ transport, timeout })` in `#connectCDP` (Browser.ts:580-581), and `AbortSignal.timeout(this.#timeout())` for the HTTP discovery (Browser.ts:531). The first case calls `connect()` twice and makes a scripted ping, and no assertion in it needs a short deadline. The second case needs a deadline only so the unanswered `Browser.getVersion` times out. `BrowserCallOptions.timeout` (src/core/types.ts:2704) already scopes a deadline to the ping, because `Browser.ping` passes its options to `client.send` (Browser.ts:153).
failure_scenario: On a loaded host, the in-process `CDPTestServer` answers the WebSocket upgrade or `/json/list` over real loopback sockets. If the event loop stalls for more than 30 ms between the request and the reply, the timers phase fires the deadline before the socket callback runs. `connect()` then rejects with a timeout, and the case fails with no code defect. The test then passes when run alone. Fix: drop `timeout` from the first case. In the second case, size the instance deadline from a full contended run (tests.md:176). Alternatively, prove that the ping inherits the deadline without starving `connect`, for example by asserting that the `CDPTimeoutError` names the configured deadline while the connect path uses a budget sized for load.

verdict.reason: The code facts hold. The instance timeout of 30 ms bounds the WebSocket upgrade and every target-sync command in `#connectCDP`, and the first case needs no short deadline. Whether a stall over 30 ms occurs in a contended `src:server` run is a host fact that reading cannot settle. The tests.md:176 budget rule is scoped to expensive proofs. The 'flake the dispatch reports' has no record in the writer reports or in the design folder. The second case needs the instance deadline because its claim is that ping inherits the client-wide deadline, so swapping in a per-call `timeout` would test a different contract.
verdict.evidence: tests/src/server/Browser.test.ts:48 and :76 pass `timeout: 30`. src/server/Browser.ts:523-524 (`#timeout`) feeds that value to :580-581 (`createCDPTransport({ url, timeout })` and `new CDPClient({ transport, timeout })`), then to :585 (`client.connect()`) and :594 (`#syncContexts()`). Every other case in the file sizes its timeout at 500 ms or more. A grep of tmp/codex/eager-*.md for 'flak' or 'timing' finds no reported U2 flake.

claim: The case 'launches one time under two concurrent first calls' still has its lazy-era body. Under the eager start it cannot fail when concurrent calls stop sharing one acquire. U6 named this case (old :71) for a rewrite, and it was not rewritten.
evidence: `await server.start()` resolves only after `#setup` holds the lease (BrowserMCPServer.ts:215 and :388). Each later call takes the held-lease branch of `#serve` (lines 406-410), so no acquire runs. `launcher.hold()` at line 1137 parks only later launches, and none happens. `waitForCondition(... launcher.browsers[0]?.connects === 1)` at line 1153 is already true, because double 0 connected during `start()`. The comment at line 1138 ('both reach their dispatchers before the launch settles') is false: the launch settled before either call was sent.
failure_scenario: Mutation: replace `this.#granting ??= ...` in `#grant` (BrowserMCPServer.ts:370) with a fresh `pool.acquire()` per caller. Both calls still find `#lease` set, ping it, and run on double 0, and every assertion passes (`browsers` has length 1 and `connects` is 1). Fix: hold the launch before `start()`, send both calls while setup is pending, release, and assert one launch with both calls answered on double 0. Alternatively, delete the case and rely on the failover case at line 630.

verdict.reason: `await server.start()` resolves only after `#setup` has awaited `#grant`, which runs `#hold` and sets `#lease`.
